Hydrogen
Henry Cavendish
England
From the Greek hydor genes, «water-former»: when it burns it produces water.
Cavendish isolated it in 1766 by reacting metals with acids and called it «inflammable air». In 1783 Lavoisier gave it its modern name after realising that burning it forms water.
It is the most abundant element in the universe (about three atoms out of four). On Earth it is found mostly bound in water and hydrocarbons.
Making ammonia for fertilisers, oil refining, fuel cells, rocket fuel, welding.
Every second the Sun «burns» about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen, turning it into helium: that is where the light that warms us comes from.
Helium
Pierre Janssen, Norman Lockyer
France / England
From the Greek helios, «Sun», because it was first seen in sunlight.
It was discovered as a mysterious yellow line in the Sun's spectrum during an 1868 eclipse. Only in 1895 did William Ramsay find it on Earth, inside a uranium mineral.
It is the second most abundant element in the universe. On Earth it is extracted from natural gas fields, where it builds up from the decay of uranium and thorium.
Cooling the magnets of MRI scanners, balloons and airships, breathing mixtures for divers, welding, leak detection.
Breathing helium makes your voice squeaky because sound travels much faster in such a light gas. It is also the only element that never freezes at normal pressure, not even at absolute zero.
Lithium
Johan August Arfwedson
Sweden
From the Greek lithos, «stone», because it was found in a mineral.
Arfwedson identified it in 1817 while analysing petalite, a mineral from the Swedish island of Utö. The pure metal was obtained by electrolysis by Bunsen and Matthiessen in 1855.
It is extracted from the brines of salt lakes (Chile, Argentina, Bolivia) and from minerals such as spodumene (Australia).
Rechargeable batteries for phones and electric cars, heat-resistant glass and ceramics, lubricating greases, medicines.
It is the lightest metal of all: it floats on water (and even on oil)! But careful, it fizzes when it touches water.
Beryllium
Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin
France
From the mineral beryl, from which it was extracted.
Vauquelin discovered beryllium oxide in 1798 while analysing beryl and emeralds. The metal was isolated in 1828 by Wöhler and Bussy.
It occurs in minerals such as beryl and bertrandite; the main producers are the United States and China.
Copper-beryllium alloys for springs and non-sparking tools, X-ray windows, the mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope.
Emerald and aquamarine are really beryl coloured by tiny impurities of chromium and iron.
Boron
Gay-Lussac and Thénard; Humphry Davy
France / England
From borax, the mineral it comes from (from the Arabic buraq).
In 1808 it was isolated almost at the same time in France by Gay-Lussac and Thénard and in England by Davy, by heating boric acid with potassium.
It occurs in borate minerals, especially in Turkey and the United States. At Larderello, in Tuscany, boric acid used to be extracted from natural steam vents.
Borosilicate glass (ovenware and lab glassware), fibreglass, detergents, fertilisers, control rods in nuclear reactors.
Plants cannot live without boron: they need it to build the walls of their cells properly.
Carbon
Known since prehistory
From the Latin carbo, «charcoal».
Charcoal and soot were used since prehistory. In 1772 Lavoisier showed that diamond is made of carbon by burning one with a lens.
It is found in coal, oil, natural gas, limestone, in the air as carbon dioxide and in every living thing.
Fuels, steel, carbon fibre, pencil graphite, diamonds for jewellery and cutting tools, activated-carbon filters.
Diamond and pencil graphite are made of the same element: only the way the atoms are bonded changes. You yourself are about 18% carbon.
Nitrogen
Daniel Rutherford
Scotland
From the Greek nitron genes, «nitre-former». In Italian and French it is called azoto, from a-zoe, «without life», because animals cannot survive in pure nitrogen.
Rutherford isolated it in 1772 by removing oxygen and carbon dioxide from air: what was left was a gas in which a candle went out.
It makes up about 78% of the air we breathe. It is also in the proteins and DNA of every living thing.
Fertilisers (ammonia), protective atmosphere for food, liquid nitrogen for freezing, explosives, airbags.
Liquid nitrogen is so cold (−196 °C) that a rose dipped in it for a few seconds becomes as brittle as glass and shatters.
Oxygen
Carl Wilhelm Scheele; Joseph Priestley
Sweden / England
From the Greek oxys genes, «acid-former»: Lavoisier wrongly believed it was present in all acids.
Scheele produced it around 1771-72 but published late; Priestley obtained it in 1774 by heating mercury oxide. Lavoisier understood its role in burning and breathing.
It is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust (almost half the weight of rocks), makes up 21% of the air and 89% of the weight of water.
Medical oxygen in hospitals, steelmaking, welding, rocket propellant (liquid oxygen), water treatment.
Liquid oxygen is pale blue and is attracted by a magnet!
Fluorine
Henri Moissan
France
From the mineral fluorite, in turn from the Latin fluere, «to flow», because it was used as a flux.
It was so reactive that several chemists were injured or killed trying to isolate it. Moissan succeeded in 1886 by electrolysis and won the Nobel Prize in 1906.
It occurs mainly in the minerals fluorite, cryolite and fluorapatite.
Toothpaste (fluorides), Teflon for non-stick pans, refrigerant gases, uranium enrichment, medicines.
It is the most reactive element of all: it can make even glass and water «burn».
Neon
William Ramsay, Morris Travers
England
From the Greek neos, «new».
Ramsay and Travers found it in 1898 by distilling liquid air: when they excited it with electricity it glowed bright red.
It is present in air in tiny amounts (about 18 parts per million) and is obtained by distilling liquid air.
Illuminated signs, helium-neon lasers, old TV tubes, cryogenic refrigerant.
The famous red «neon» signs really are neon; signs of other colours use other gases or fluorescent powders.
Sodium
Humphry Davy
England
From soda; the symbol Na comes from the Latin natrium.
Davy isolated it in 1807 by passing an electric current through molten caustic soda: it was one of the first elements obtained by electrolysis.
It is very abundant: in table salt, seawater and many minerals.
Table salt, yellow street lamps, soap, glass, cooling some nuclear reactors.
Pure sodium is a soft metal you can cut with a knife, and if you drop it in water it explodes! Combined with chlorine, also poisonous, it forms the salt we eat.
Magnesium
Humphry Davy
England
From Magnesia, a region of Greece rich in minerals.
Joseph Black recognised it as an element in 1755; Davy isolated it in 1808 by electrolysis.
It occurs in dolomite (the Dolomites are named after this mineral), magnesite and seawater.
Light alloys for cars, planes and bikes, fireworks, old photographic flashes, supplements, chlorophyll.
Every molecule of chlorophyll, which makes leaves green, has a magnesium atom at its centre.
Aluminium
Hans Christian Ørsted
Denmark
From alum, a salt used since ancient times.
Ørsted obtained a small amount in 1825; Wöhler produced it better in 1827. In 1886 Hall and Héroult invented the electrolysis that made it cheap.
It is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust. It is extracted from bauxite (Australia, Guinea, China).
Cans, kitchen foil, aircraft, cars, window frames, power cables, pans.
In the 1800s it was worth more than gold: Napoleon III served his most important guests with aluminium cutlery. The tip of the Washington Monument is made of aluminium.
Silicon
Jöns Jacob Berzelius
Sweden
From the Latin silex, «flint».
Berzelius isolated it in 1824 by heating potassium fluorosilicate with potassium.
It is the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust: sand, quartz and almost all rocks contain silicon.
Chips and processors, solar panels, glass, cement, silicones, aluminium alloys.
Silicon Valley in California is named after this element: every computer and smartphone has a «brain» made of ultra-pure silicon.
Phosphorus
Hennig Brand
Germany
From the Greek phosphoros, «light-bearer».
Brand, an alchemist from Hamburg, was looking for the philosopher's stone by boiling huge amounts of urine. Instead he got a substance that glowed in the dark.
It occurs in phosphate rocks (Morocco, China, United States), in bones and in DNA.
Fertilisers, matches, detergents, special steels, soft drinks (phosphoric acid), semiconductors.
It was the first element discovered by a person whose name we know. White phosphorus glows in the dark when exposed to air.
Sulfur
Known since antiquity
From the Latin sulfur.
It was known in antiquity: the Bible calls it «brimstone», the burning stone. In 1777 Lavoisier showed that it is an element.
It is found near volcanoes (Sicily once had large sulfur mines) and is mostly recovered today from refining oil and gas.
Sulfuric acid (the most produced chemical in the world), fertilisers, rubber vulcanisation, matches, gunpowder.
The rotten-egg smell is not pure sulfur but hydrogen sulfide, one of its compounds.
Chlorine
Carl Wilhelm Scheele
Sweden
From the Greek chloros, «pale green», for the colour of the gas.
Scheele produced it in 1774 but thought it was a compound. Davy showed in 1810 that it was an element.
It occurs in salt (sodium chloride), seawater and rock-salt deposits.
Disinfecting drinking water and swimming pools, PVC, bleach, medicines.
The «swimming-pool smell» is not chlorine itself but substances formed when chlorine reacts with sweat.
Argon
Lord Rayleigh, William Ramsay
England
From the Greek argos, «lazy, inert», because it hardly reacts with anything.
Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen taken from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made chemically. With Ramsay he found a hidden gas: argon. Both won Nobel Prizes in 1904.
It is the third most abundant gas in air (almost 1%).
Shielding gas for welding, light bulbs, double glazing, preserving old documents.
In whatever room you are in there are several litres of argon: air contains more argon than carbon dioxide.
Potassium
Humphry Davy
England
From potash (plant ashes in a pot); the symbol K comes from the Latin kalium.
It was the first metal isolated by electrolysis: in 1807 Davy saw little beads of metal that crackled and caught fire.
It is extracted from salt deposits such as sylvite (Canada, Russia, Belarus).
Fertilisers, soap, glass, nutrition: it is essential for nerves and muscles.
Bananas are famous for their potassium. A piece of potassium metal dropped in water burns with a violet flame.
Calcium
Humphry Davy
England
From the Latin calx, «lime».
Lime was already used by the Romans; Davy isolated the metal in 1808 by electrolysis.
Very abundant: limestone, marble, gypsum, shells, bones and teeth.
Cement and lime for building, plaster, milk and cheese (for bones), steelmaking.
Carrara marble, cave stalactites and eggshells are all made of calcium carbonate.
Scandium
Lars Fredrik Nilson
Sweden
From Scandinavia.
Mendeleev had predicted it in 1871, calling it «eka-boron». Nilson discovered it in 1879 in Scandinavian minerals, confirming the prediction.
It is rare and scattered; it is obtained as a by-product of other mining, for example uranium.
Aluminium-scandium alloys for bicycles and baseball bats, metal-halide stadium lamps.
It was one of the first proofs that Mendeleev's periodic table could «predict the future».
Titanium
William Gregor
England
From the Titans of Greek mythology.
Reverend Gregor found it in 1791 in the black sand of a Cornish stream. Klaproth rediscovered it in 1795 and named it.
It is extracted from minerals such as rutile and ilmenite (Australia, South Africa, China).
Aircraft, prostheses and dental implants, glasses frames, bicycles; titanium dioxide is the white in paints and toothpaste.
It is as strong as steel but weighs almost half as much, and our body accepts it without problems: that is why it is used for implants.
Vanadium
Andrés Manuel del Río; Nils Sefström
Mexico / Sweden
From Vanadís, the Norse goddess of beauty, for the beautiful colours of its compounds.
Del Río discovered it in Mexico in 1801 but was persuaded that he had made a mistake. Sefström rediscovered it in Sweden in 1830.
It occurs in minerals such as vanadinite and magnetite; main producers are China, Russia and South Africa.
Special steels for tools and springs, flow batteries for storing energy.
Spanners stamped «Cr-V» are made of chromium-vanadium steel.
Chromium
Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin
France
From the Greek chroma, «colour», for the bright colours of its compounds.
Vauquelin discovered it in 1797 while studying a red mineral from Siberia, crocoite.
It is extracted from chromite (South Africa, Kazakhstan, Turkey).
Stainless steel, shiny chrome plating, pigments, leather tanning.
The red of rubies and the green of emeralds both come from traces of chromium.
Manganese
Johan Gottlieb Gahn
Sweden
From magnesia nigra, a black mineral.
Scheele realised in 1774 that it was a new element; the same year his colleague Gahn isolated the metal.
It occurs in pyrolusite (South Africa, Australia, Gabon) and in nodules on the ocean floor.
Steel, alkaline batteries, aluminium-alloy cans, fertilisers.
On the ocean floor there are billions of metal «potatoes» called manganese nodules.
Iron
Known since prehistory
From the Old English iren; the symbol Fe comes from the Latin ferrum.
Meteoritic iron was already used 5,000 years ago; the Iron Age began about 3,200 years ago, when people learned to extract it from ores.
It is the fourth element of the Earth's crust and makes up most of the Earth's core. It is extracted from hematite and magnetite (Australia, Brazil).
Steel for buildings, cars, ships and tools: it is the most used metal in the world. In blood it carries oxygen.
Blood is red thanks to the iron in haemoglobin. And the Earth is a giant magnet because its core is made of molten iron.
Cobalt
Georg Brandt
Sweden
From the German Kobold, a goblin of the mines.
German miners called «Kobold» the ores that looked like copper but did not yield it. In 1735 Brandt showed that they contained a new metal.
It is mined mostly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as a by-product of copper and nickel.
Lithium batteries, superalloys for jet engines, magnets, cobalt-blue pigment, vitamin B12.
The blue of ancient Chinese porcelain and of Gothic stained-glass windows comes from cobalt.
Nickel
Axel Fredrik Cronstedt
Sweden
From the German Kupfernickel, «devil's copper».
Miners thought a reddish ore contained copper bewitched by a goblin (Nickel). In 1751 Cronstedt discovered that it contained a new metal.
It is mined in Indonesia, the Philippines and Russia; it is abundant in the Earth's core and in meteorites.
Stainless steel, coins, batteries, plating, magnets.
The American 5-cent coin is actually called a «nickel».
Copper
Known since prehistory
From the Latin aes cyprium, «metal of Cyprus», an island famous for its mines. The symbol Cu comes from cuprum.
It was one of the first metals used by humans, over 10,000 years ago. Ötzi the Iceman carried a copper axe.
It is mined in Chile, Peru, Congo and China, from minerals such as chalcopyrite and malachite.
Electric wires, pipes, motors, coins, bronze (copper and tin) and brass (copper and zinc).
The Statue of Liberty is made of copper: it was shiny orange and turned green over time because of its patina.
Zinc
Andreas Marggraf
Germany
Probably from the German Zinke, «prong», for the shape of its crystals.
It was already produced in India in the 12th century. In Europe Marggraf isolated and described it in 1746.
It is extracted from sphalerite (China, Peru, Australia).
Galvanising iron against rust, brass, batteries, sunscreens, supplements.
White sunscreens contain zinc oxide, which acts as a mirror for the Sun's rays.
